author: Origen of Alexandria
occasion: Explanatory notes on difficult or noteworthy passages in the Greek text of Judges, addressing apparent moral problems, dialect terms, and the meaning of customs and objects.
argument: Origen defends the Spirit's role in Jephthah's vow by distinguishing divine assistance from human error. He explains the pronunciation test as a dialect difference that exposed enemies, using the Greek terms σέβηλα and σεβήλω. He interprets Manoah's wife's barrenness as temporary and functional rather than natural. He connects Samson's hair to his Nazirite consecration and strength, and explains the ephod and theraphin as priestly versus idolatrous objects. Finally, he argues that the Benjamites' initial defeats were a just punishment for a prior cause, with victory coming only after wrath had been satisfied.

outline.move: Explains that the Spirit helped Jephthah but did not prompt his rash vow.
Explains the pronunciation test as a dialect difference that exposed Ephraimites.
Interprets the barrenness of Manoah's wife as temporary and functional, not natural.
Shows that Samson's hair was the source of his strength throughout his story.
Explains that 'Nazirite' means 'the guarded one' in Syrian, and that God commanded Samson not to follow the Israelite custom of shaving the head to be conspicuous.
Distinguishes the priestly ephod from the idolatrous theraphin.
Argues that the Benjamites' defeats were just punishment for a prior cause, with victory coming only after wrath was satisfied.

key_terms.sense: The Spirit of the Lord that came upon Jephthah to help him
Jephthah's vow or promise to God
The test word 'ear of grain' used to distinguish Ephraimites by pronunciation
The correct pronunciation of the test word meaning 'ear of grain'
The Ephraimites' mispronunciation of the test word, exposing them as enemies
The agreed password or test word
Barren, but here meaning temporarily childless by divine arrangement
A person consecrated to God, marked by uncut hair; Origen says it means 'the guarded one' in Syrian
Samson's hair, the visible sign and source of his strength
A priestly woven garment through which the grace of the Holy Spirit came
An idolatrous object, not divine, as shown in the books of Kingdoms
Divine wrath that fell on the wrongdoers before the Benjamites' victory

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: σημαίνει σέβηλα, ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἄσταχυς. Οἱ δὲ ἔλεγον σεβήλω... Τὸ οὖν σύνθεμα ἦν σέβηλα, ὅπερ οἱ ἐπερωτώμενοι λέγοντες σεδήλω
_unresolved_facts.fix: using the Greek terms σέβηλα and σεβήλω/σεδήλω (the source has both σεβήλω and σεδήλω)

_unresolved_facts.claim: Shows that Samson's hair was the source of his strength throughout his story
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Δι᾿ ὅλης τῆς περὶ τὸν Σαμψὼν ἱστορίας αἱ τρίχες φαίνονται τὴν πᾶσαν αὐτῷ περιποιεῖν ἰσχύν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Shows that Samson's hair appears to preserve all his strength throughout his story

_unresolved_facts.claim: Explains that 'Nazirite' means 'the guarded one' in Syrian, and that God commanded Samson not to follow the Israelite custom of shaving the head to be conspicuous
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ναζιραῖον τὸ πεφυλαγμένον κατὰ τὴν Σύρων φωνὴν ὀνομάζει. Μὴ ἐξακολουθεῖν δὲ τῇ τάξει τῶν Ἰσραηλιτῶν τὸν Σαμψὼν ὁ Θεὸς προστάσσει, κατ᾿ ἐκεῖνο καιροῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν ξυρωμένων διὰ τὸ εὐσήμους εἶναι πρὸς πάντας
_unresolved_facts.fix: Explains that 'Nazirite' means 'the guarded one' in Syrian, and that God commanded Samson not to follow the Israelite custom of that time, when they shaved their heads to be conspicuous to all
